## The incident

In May 2014 the Office for National Statistics published how illegal drugs and prostitution would enter UK GDP. The reason, per the article by Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew: gross national income "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget".

The rule was older: ESA95 already included consensual illegal transactions. ONS's footnote: "There are no changes in this area between ESA95 and ESA10."

The prostitution estimate starts in London in 2004. The charity Eaves "estimated that there were approx 7000 off-street prostitutes in London in that year; this was done by calling numbers advertised in various media and asking how many prostitutes were in each place". The Metropolitan Police supplied "115 prostitutes on the street at any one time in London". Scaled up by UK population, that "gives c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country."

Clients per week followed "a Netherlands assumption with some research support": estimates based on 20, 25 and 30. The price, £55 in 2004, was "an estimate from Punternet supported by a 2004 journal article". Footnote 12, for Punternet, is a Wikipedia URL.

"As there is no time series, we vary the point estimates in time using the male population". ONS called this "a weak assumption".

## Who lied

Nobody. Every assumption was published, and several were graded by the people who made them.

On drugs: "We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption." On production: "We assume that no drugs other than cannabis are produced in the UK. While this is probably false, we do not have any evidence to the contrary." "Probably false" appears 3 times in the article.

1 assumption was rated reasonable: "The government final consumption expenditure assumption is reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."

The article "does not include numerical impacts". In an October 2014 Civil Service Quarterly blog, Peter Patterson, ONS Deputy Chief Economic Adviser, wrote that "ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!)" put the contribution at "up to £10 billion a year".

## The bit continues

ONS's Blue Book 2016 revisions article reduced the prostitution estimate "by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes. Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

An ONS Freedom of Information reply gave prostitution in 2010 as "£5.6bn (current prices), which is 0.4% of GDP." Today's series, MNC8, gives 2010 as £4,370m. By this site's arithmetic, the ratio is 0.78, and 40 weeks out of 52 is 0.77. ONS does not say the holiday is the whole difference.

MNC8 starts in 1985, 29 years before the first estimate was published. It shows £5,993m in 2019, £4,130m in 2020 and £6,431m in 2024. The latest release was 31 October 2025.

## The incident

In May 2014 the Office for National Statistics (ONS) published how it would add illegal drugs and prostitution to the UK national accounts. The rule was not new: the European System of National Accounts 1995 counts "illegal transactions to which all units involved consent" within the production boundary. The timing came from an audit. Gross national income "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget", and in 2012 "a number of areas for improvement were identified which Member States have to address by 2014."

The charity Eaves estimated about 7,000 off-street prostitutes in London in 2004, "by calling numbers advertised in various media and asking how many prostitutes were in each place". The Metropolitan Police gave "115 prostitutes on the street at any one time in London". Adding these and scaling up by UK population "gives c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country." Clients per week follow "a Netherlands assumption with some research support": 20, 25 and 30. The price, £55 in 2004, is "an estimate from Punternet supported by a 2004 journal article". The footnote for Punternet links to Wikipedia.

Over time, the number moves with the 16+ male population. ONS: "This is a weak assumption ... It is necessary because we have no time series data for the number of prostitutes."

For drugs: "We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption." The assumption on government spending "is reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS published every assumption and labelled several itself. The phrase "probably false" appears 3 times in the article, and "arbitrary" twice. On drug purity: "This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it."

Peter Patterson, ONS Deputy Chief Economic Adviser, wrote on the Civil Service Quarterly blog in October 2014: "ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!) into the numbers of prostitutes and the price of drugs yielded the result that spending on these illegal activities in the UK contributes up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP."

## The bit continues

In Blue Book 2016, ONS reduced the prostitution estimates "by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes. Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

An ONS freedom of information reply gives prostitution in 2010 as £5.6bn. Series MNC8, last released 31 October 2025, gives £4,370m. This site's arithmetic, not ONS's: £4,370m is 78% of £5.6bn, and 40 weeks are 77% of 52. None of the ONS sources here says the holiday is the whole difference.

MNC8 begins in 1985, 29 years before ONS first published an estimate. In 2020 it fell 31%, from £5,993m to £4,130m. In 2024 it stood at £6,431m.

"We assume that the purity-adjusted amount of drugs consumed by the average user remains constant over time. This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it." "We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption." "The government final consumption expenditure assumption is reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs." "Probably false" appears 3 times.

Prostitution has no time series. The charity Eaves estimated approx 7000 off-street prostitutes in London in 2004 by calling advertised numbers. The Metropolitan Police gave 115 on the street. The count is then moved through time with the male population, which ONS calls "a weak assumption".

Peter Patterson, ONS Deputy Chief Economic Adviser, wrote on the Civil Service Quarterly blog that "ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!)" produced a contribution of "up to £10 billion a year" to GDP. ## The incident

In May 2014 ONS published "Changes to National Accounts: Inclusion of Illegal Drugs and Prostitution in the UK National Accounts", by Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew. The reason was the EU budget. Gross national income "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget", and a 2012 audit had flagged areas to fix by 2014.

The rule was not new. The European System of National Accounts 1995 includes "illegal transactions to which all units involved consent" within the production boundary.

The prostitution estimate starts with a headcount. Eaves, a charity, phoned advertised numbers in 2004 and estimated approx 7000 off-street prostitutes in London. The Metropolitan Police counted 115 on the street at any one time. Adding them and scaling by UK population gives "c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country."

The 2004 point estimate is then varied by the male population: "As there is no time series, we vary the point estimates in time using the male population." Clients per week were calculated on 20, 25 and 30, "Following a Netherlands assumption with some research support". The text does not say which was used. The price was £55 in 2004, from Punternet. Footnote 12 for that price links to a Wikipedia page.

The assumption that drug consumption per user stays constant over time: "This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it." Half of cannabis is assumed imported: "This is an arbitrary assumption." The government assumption is "reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."

In October 2014 Peter Patterson, ONS's deputy chief economic adviser, wrote on a government blog that spending on these activities "contributes up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP". The overall effect, he wrote, was "to raise the level of GDP by around £50 billion a year", some 4%.

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS published each assumption and labelled the weak ones. The article calls its own inputs "probably false", "an arbitrary assumption" and "a weak assumption". It says its estimates are "partly based" on assumptions, and that this "applies especially" to prostitution.

## The bit continues

In 2016 the Blue Book revisions added a holiday. ONS reduced the prostitution estimates "by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes". Statistics Netherlands had estimated "the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year", and "the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

An FOI reply put 2010 prostitution at £5.6bn, at current prices. The current MNC8 series gives £4,370m for the same year. This site's arithmetic: £4,370m is 78% of £5.6bn, and 40 working weeks in 52 is 77%. ONS does not state that the holiday accounts for the whole difference.

The series starts at £1,078m in 1985. Its first estimate was published in 2014, and it is modelled, not observed. It falls to £4,130m in 2020, from £5,993m in 2019.

## The incident

On 29 May 2014 ONS published how illegal drugs and prostitution would enter the UK national accounts. Its article notes that the European System of National Accounts 1995 "states that illegal transactions to which all units involved consent are included within the production boundary". Gross national income, it adds, "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget". A 2012 audit of methods across EU countries had found "a number of areas for improvement", to be addressed by 2014.

For prostitution, annual volume is "P\*C\*52": prostitutes, times clients a week, times 52 weeks. P starts with a 2004 estimate by Eaves, a charity: "approx 7000 off-street prostitutes in London"; "this was done by calling numbers advertised in various media and asking how many prostitutes were in each place". The Metropolitan Police figure was "115 prostitutes on the street at any one time in London". "Adding these and scaling up by UK population ... gives c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country." For C, "Following a Netherlands assumption with some research support", ONS calculated estimates at 20, 25 and 30 clients a week.

The price, £55 in 2004, is "an estimate from Punternet supported by a 2004 journal article". Footnote 12, for Punternet, is a Wikipedia link. For other years: "As there is no time series, we vary the point estimates in time using the male population". The series ONS publishes, MNC8, begins in 1985.

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS published the assumptions and its own assessment of them. Assumption 1 is that "the number of prostitutes has the same pattern through time as the 16+ male population. This is a weak assumption".

Table 3, on drugs: "We assume that the purity-adjusted amount of drugs consumed by the average user remains constant over time. This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it." "We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption." "The government final consumption expenditure assumption is reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs." The article uses "probably false" 3 times.

In October 2014 Peter Patterson, ONS's Deputy Chief Economic Adviser, wrote in Civil Service Quarterly that "ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!)" found spending on drugs and prostitution "contributes up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP".

## The bit continues

In 2016 ONS reduced the prostitution estimates "by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes. Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

An ONS freedom of information reply gives prostitution spending in 2010 as £5.6bn. MNC8 now gives the same year as £4,370m. By this site's arithmetic, not ONS's: £4,370m is 78% of £5.6bn, and 40 of 52 weeks is 77%.

In 2020 the series fell from £5,993m to £4,130m. By 2024 it was £6,431m.

## The incident

In May 2014 the Office for National Statistics (ONS) published how it would add illegal drugs and prostitution to the UK national accounts. The article, by Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew, gave the reason. Gross national income "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget", and a 2012 audit of EU methods had found "a number of areas for improvement" to address by 2014. The rule was older: ESA95 section 1.13 counts illegal transactions "to which all units involved consent". ONS's footnote: "There are no changes in this area between ESA95 and ESA10."

The data, the article said, had "significant limitations", which "requires a number of assumptions on which the estimates are, therefore, partly based. This applies especially to the estimates of prostitution activity."

The prostitution method multiplied prostitutes, clients and price by 52. In 2004 the charity Eaves "estimated that there were approx 7000 off-street prostitutes in London in that year; this was done by calling numbers advertised in various media and asking how many prostitutes were in each place". The Metropolitan Police counted "115 prostitutes on the street at any one time in London". Scaled up by UK population: "c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country." Clients per week followed "a Netherlands assumption with some research support": estimates on 20, 25 and 30. The price, £55 in 2004, came from Punternet. Punternet's footnote is a Wikipedia URL.

"As there is no time series", the 2004 figures were moved with the 16+ male population. ONS: "This is a weak assumption."

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS published every assumption and graded it.

"We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption."

"We assume that the purity-adjusted amount of drugs consumed by the average user remains constant over time. This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it." The phrase "probably false" appears 3 times in the article.

Government spending on drugs was set aside "because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."

"There is no employment in prostitution; all prostitutes and pimps are self-employed. This is a controversial assumption".

## The bit continues

An ONS freedom-of-information reply put illegal production in 2010 at £9,097m, 0.58% of GDP. It gave prostitution spending for 2010 as £5.6bn.

In Blue Book 2016, ONS reduced the prostitution estimates "by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes. Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

Series MNC8 now gives 2010 as £4,370m. By this site's arithmetic, not ONS's, £4,370m is 78% of £5.6bn, and a 40-week year is 77% of 52 weeks. ONS does not say the holiday is the whole difference.

The series begins in 1985, 29 years before ONS's first estimate.

original.body:
## The incident

In 2014 the UK added illegal drugs and prostitution to its national accounts. Gross national income "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget", and a 2012 audit of EU methods had identified areas for improvement "which Member States have to address by 2014."

The rule was not new. ESA95, section 1.13, "states that illegal transactions to which all units involved consent are included within the production boundary". ONS added: "There are no changes in this area between ESA95 and ESA10."

ONS published the method on 29 May 2014, by Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew. It warned of "significant limitations in the availability of data", requiring assumptions on which the estimates are "partly based". "This applies especially to the estimates of prostitution activity."

The count started in London in 2004. A charity, Eaves, estimated about 7,000 off-street prostitutes, "by calling numbers advertised in various media and asking how many prostitutes were in each place". The Metropolitan Police counted 115 on the street "at any one time". Scaled by population, that "gives c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country." Clients per week followed "a Netherlands assumption", run at 20, 25 and 30. The price, £55 in 2004, came from Punternet. Footnote 12, for Punternet, is a Wikipedia URL.

The drugs section graded its own work. Constant consumption per user: "This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it." Half of cannabis imported, half home-grown: "This is an arbitrary assumption." No government spending on drugs: "reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."

## Who lied

Nobody. Every assumption was published, and most arrived labelled. "Probably false" appears 3 times in the article; "arbitrary", twice. Tracking prostitution through time by the 16+ male population is "a weak assumption", needed "because we have no time series data for the number of prostitutes". Treating every prostitute and pimp as self-employed is "a controversial assumption".

In October 2014 Peter Patterson, ONS Deputy Chief Economic Adviser, wrote on the Civil Service Quarterly blog that "ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!)" put the contribution at "up to £10 billion a year". The change was "legally mandated", and "Comparability between nations dictates that all countries include it in their GDP figures."

## The bit continues

Blue Book 2016 reduced the prostitution estimates "to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes". "Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

An ONS freedom of information reply gives prostitution in 2010 as "£5.6bn (current prices)". Series MNC8 now gives 2010 as £4,370m. ONS does not attribute the difference. This site's arithmetic: £4,370m is 78% of £5.6bn, and 40 weeks is 77% of 52.

MNC8 was last released on 31 October 2025. It shows £5,993m for 2019, £4,130m for 2020 and £6,431m for 2024.
